{{Short description|English mathematician and physician (1556–1620)}}

{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2025}}
{{Use British English|date=July 2016}}
'''Thomas Hood''' (1556 – 1620) was an English [[mathematician]] and [[physician]], the first lecturer in mathematics appointed in England, a few years before the founding of [[Gresham College]]. He publicized the [[Copernican theory]], and discussed the nova [[SN 1572]].<ref name="Kanas07">{{cite book|author=Kanas, Nick  |title=Star Maps: History, Artistry, and Cartography|url=https://archive.org/details/starmapshistorya00mdpr  |url-access=limited  |year=2007|pages=[https://archive.org/details/starmapshistorya00mdpr/page/n171 146]–47|isbn=978-0-387-71668-8|publisher=Praxis Publishing|location=Chichester, United Kingdom}}</ref> (Tycho's Nova).  He also innovated in the design of mathematical and astronomical instruments.

==Life==
He entered [[Trinity College, Cambridge]] in 1573, and graduated B.A. in 1578; he was elected to a fellowship in the same year, and graduated M.A. in 1581.<ref>{{acad|id=HT573T|name=Hood, Thomas}}</ref> His Cambridge licence to practice as a physician was from 1585. He was approached to lecture in mathematics in 1582, by the merchant [[Thomas Smythe]]. The lectures in fact began in 1588.<ref name = RB>[[W. W. Rouse Ball]], ''A History of the Study of Mathematics at Cambridge'' (1889), pp. 23–4.</ref><ref>''Concise Dictionary of National Biography''</ref>

He lectured from 1588 to 1592. The applications in view were military (intended for Captains of train bands, in other words for militia commanders at the time of the [[Spanish Armada]]), and subsequently aimed at naval needs and navigation. The first lectures were in the Staples Inn Chapel, but the regular venue became Smythe's London house, [[Leadenhall]] in Gracechurch Street. Other supporters of the lectures were [[John Wolstenholme (merchant)|Sir John Wolstenholme]] and [[John Lumley, 1st Baron Lumley]]; Hood was a subscriber in 1589 to the [[Virginia Company]], with which his merchant backers were associated. Hood's original publications were probably derived from notes of the talks. He collaborated with the engraver [[Augustine Ryther]] on both celestial and terrestrial charts.<ref name =RB/><ref>Eric H. Ash, ''Power, Knowledge, and Expertise in Elizabethan England'' (2004), p. 158.</ref><ref>[[Christopher Hill (historian)|Christopher Hill]], ''Intellectual Origins of the English Revolution'' (1967), pp. 33 and p. 78.</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/EPACT/maker.php?MakerID=23 | title=Epact: Scientific Instruments of Medieval and Renaissance Europe }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gresham.ac.uk/printtranscript.asp?EventId=825|title=Gresham College|access-date=22 February 2009|archive-date=25 November 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101125095035/http://gresham.ac.uk/printtranscript.asp?EventId=825|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In later life he lived in [[Candlewick (ward)|Abchurch Lane, London]], practiced as a physician, and sold copies of his hemisphere charts.<ref>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Hood, Thomas (fl.1582-1598)|volume=27}}</ref>

==Works==
*''A Copie of the Speache ...'' (1588)
*''The Use of the Celestial Globe in Plano, set forth in two hemispheres'' (1590)
*''The Use of Jacobs Staffe''
*''Making and Use of the Sector''
*''Elementes of Geometrie'' (1590), translated from the Latin of [[Petrus Ramus]], ''Geometriae Septem Et Viginti''
*A translation of the arithmetic of [[Christian Wursteisen]] (1596)
*Work on surveying (1598).
